title: What curtilage actually is
paras: Let's start with what curtilage actually is. There's no statutory definition — it's all case law. The idea is land forming one enclosure with the house, the same physical and functional unit, walled or not. Three factors, none decisive alone: the physical layout, the relationship between house and land; ownership, past and present; and use or function. And it needn't be small — relationship, not size: a walled garden can sit wholly within, a paddock across a track outside.

Now, what it's not. Not the red line on your plan, not the extent of ownership, not just what's mown — you can own ten acres without ten acres of curtilage. Nor is domestic use conclusive: in Burford, land used for purposes incidental to the house was still held outside the curtilage — fenced off, not one enclosure with it. Incidental use is a related test, but a distinct one.

The planning role is specific and unforgiving. Curtilage defines the land within which permitted development rights operate — a building outside it needs express permission, however small — and it decides enforcement the same way. In listed building law it fixes what a listing catches: an unnamed structure within the curtilage at the time of listing is protected, on a tighter threshold still — an intimate association, not mere proximity. Otherwise it's fact and degree, site by site — adjacency, enclosure, domestic use versus recreation at arm's length, whether it reads as garden or leftover paddock — and inspectors return, again and again, to separation and domestic character.

title: The annex as loophole
paras: Now, the annex as a loophole. 'Annex' has no protected meaning — it's a strategy now, not a description. It carries emotional and political cover — care, family, support — while dodging everything a new dwelling triggers: housing policy assessment, local plan targets, affordable housing thresholds, infrastructure contributions, the community infrastructure levy. The question is always the same — does the accommodation stay ancillary to the main house, or has it become an independent planning unit? That's judged by function and the relationship between the occupations, never by labels or kitchens.

The policy landscape invites it. National policy doesn't define annexes, and most local plans are silent or offer one-line criteria that are easy to write and impossible to apply, so it falls to officer discretion. The compassion card works, and the policy reasoning fades — usually genuine, but planning is land-use, not welfare. And the arrangement always changes — the parent dies, the annex empties, and in comes the application to formalise the dwelling as a fallback from the authority's own approval. Across hundreds of cases that's a shadow stock of homes — outside the supply figures, section 106, the levy and any oversight.

Where the principle's accepted, control comes through conditions and obligations, and most fail through laziness. A condition must pass the six tests — necessary, relevant to planning, relevant to the development, enforceable, precise and reasonable — and the recycled favourite, 'used only incidentally' or 'occupied only by family members', fails several at once: what's a family member, and how do you monitor it? Where separation is significant and the occupancy limit is the very thing making the scheme acceptable, a section 106 does what a condition can't — occupancy restrictions, non-severance and reversion clauses, ties against a separate address or services — binding on the land and successors. But it too must be necessary, directly related, and fairly and reasonably related in scale; it can't make unacceptable development acceptable, and you don't reach for an obligation where a condition would do.

title: When an annex becomes a house
paras: So when does an annex become a house? The material change of use, from ancillary annex to independent dwelling, is defined by function, not features — not a kitchen, a letterbox or rent changing hands, but the accommodation being used independently: sleeping, cooking and daily life as a separate household. In Moore, the Court of Appeal held that sleeping accommodation alone doesn't create a separate planning unit; what matters is whether the character of the use has materially changed. Facilities are evidence, but the pattern of occupation decides — shared meals, real dependence, whether it would carry on as a home without the host.

Structure and use are separate questions, and conflating them loses cases both ways. A building lawfully put up under permitted development isn't entitled to any use the owner fancies — the lawful structure doesn't legitimise an unlawful use, so the 'you can't touch it, we built it lawfully' argument fails where the rights never applied, were withdrawn, or the use can't be reverted. Equally, enforcement must allege the right breach — use, structure, or both — and a notice against a lawful structure, when the breach is the use, invites quashing. And the change is usually creep, not conversion: a run of small indicators — a shower, a kitchenette, council tax — no one of them decisive, together pointing to independent occupation.

Two modern fronts widen the same battle. The garden office: working from home isn't the issue — the tipping point is regular client or customer visits, signage, deliveries and noise, and scale. The test is the character of the use, not harm or popularity, so a materially different use needs permission even if nobody objects. And the short let: the courts recognised, before any legislation, that intensive holiday letting can be a material change of use, turning on intensity, turnover, and whether the property still behaves like a home. Government has now confirmed a dedicated short-term let use class, C5, with a national register and permitted development removable by an Article 4 direction — worth checking commencement and the local Article 4 stance.

And to regularise an independent use with a certificate, everything turns on evidence and time. The four-year rule's gone — breaches carry the ten-year period, with the old four years surviving only where the immunity accrued, or the breach happened, before a 2024 cut-off that's in the written guide. So a recent dwelling now has to prove a full decade, and legacy applications citing four years need checking against the transitional rules. The burden's on the applicant, on the balance of probabilities, across a continuous documented chain — utilities, council tax, tenancies, the electoral roll, dated neighbour statements. And Welwyn Hatfield stands over it: deliberate concealment defeats the claim — time can't immunise a dwelling hidden from the authority, and a certificate can't reward deception.

title: Certificates: facts, not feelings
paras: Finally, certificates — facts, not feelings. Two kinds: one prospective — if I do this, will it be lawful? — one retrospective — I did this, is it lawful now, either because it never needed permission or the enforcement period has run? Either way the key word is lawful, not acceptable or sensible or policy-supported. The authority doesn't investigate, weigh policy or balance harm; it tests the claim. If the evidence establishes it, the certificate must be issued; if not, refused, however sympathetic the circumstances. Binary, and the onus is entirely on the applicant, on the balance of probabilities.

It's the most misused process in planning — people assume longevity plus a trusted builder equals a rubber stamp, but certificates deal in facts: objective, consistent evidence, the standard a tax inspector would take seriously, not a persuasive planning statement. Two failures recur: continuity gaps, occupied a year then empty then short-let; and shared services, access and meals that show no real independence from the main house. The longer the period claimed, the higher the burden of proving it unbroken. And with the four-year rule gone, dwelling-certificate evidence has effectively doubled — and concealment invalidates the claim regardless of time served.

And a certificate is not a formality — granting one has consequences beyond the site. Every annex certified as a dwelling enters the housing stock without going through the plan-led process; the ancillary-use conditions fall away; future control over sub-division, letting and extension weakens; and cumulatively, a village's worth of certificates adds homes with no infrastructure reckoning. So the officer's discipline: rigour at validation, the full evidence set before the clock starts; site visits mapping layout, services and behaviour; alertness to concealment; precise refusals; and a register of these certificates revisited over time, because certified sites drift too.
